extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society; natural philosophers, observational scientists and instrument-makers (17th-century astronomers, microscopists, acousticians)
extracted.subtask_description: Recording and reporting observational/experimental findings across astronomy, microscopy, and acoustics: how to sample, observe, measure, and narrate phenomena (ephemerides, microscropy counts, acoustic experiments) for learned readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational record of Saturn's satellites visibility and phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Document when a satellite is visible or invisible through its orbit (e.g., 'visible in its greatest occidental digression, and invisible in its greatest oriental elongation'), noting positions relative to Saturn (digressions, conjunctions) and latitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the pattern of apparitions and disappearances across revolutions; note whether the satellite is seen in upper or lower parts of its circle; give distances from Saturn's centre in diameters of its ring; specify the relation of visibility to orbital phase (e.g., appears 2–3 days before conjunction, disappears 2–3 days after). Use such records to characterise visibility cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of orbital period by successive observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine a satellite's period by observing it on successive nights (example: observing 13 days successively to determine the period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make continuous successive observations across multiple revolutions where possible; record dates/times of consecutive sightings to calculate precise orbital periods (e.g., 4 days, 12 hours, and 27 minutes). Ensure observations span times when satellite reappears after invisibility to confirm periodicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer surface albedo heterogeneity from phase changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use changes in apparent magnitude/visibility with orbital phase to infer that parts of a satellite's surface reflect light differently ('one part of its surface is not so capable of reflecting to us the light of the sun as the other part is').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare visibility at different elongations and conjunctions; infer hemisphere differences (analogy to earth: sea versus continent) and consider rotation or tidal locking/exposure to the primary as explanatory mechanisms for alternating visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument aperture and capability required for detecting faint bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Note the necessary instrument size/sensitivity for discovering small/faint planets: 'the apparent magnitude of these planets is so little... their discovery was begun by a glass of 17 feet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the telescope/optical used (length, aperture, magnification) when claiming discovery of faint objects; acknowledge limits of smaller instruments when explaining previous non-detections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content elements for a philosophical essay on music
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper philosophical essay on music should explain 'the cause of sound', define 'what a tone is', describe the useful tones within a scale, relations of tones and union of mixed sounds, how tones are produced by instruments, and discuss harmony, formality, conformity, and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the work by: (1) inquiring into the physical cause of sound and core phenomena; (2) defining tones and scales; (3) explaining instrument mechanics (strings, pipes, bells) and pulse generation; (4) treating harmony (grateful joining of tones), formality (succeeding notes agreeable to former), conformity (each part's tendency), and time/measure (relation of strokes to memory). Include pertinent observations and examples (pendulums, trumpets, theatre acoustics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental procedure for observing sympathetic string vibrations
rubrics_metrics.description: When one string is sounded, another string (unison, octave, etc.) will tremble only in particular segments corresponding to the unison parts; 'not the whole of that other string trembles, but the several parts severally.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To detect which parts tremble: wrap a little bit of paper lightly about the string and remove it successively from one end to the other to observe motion; experiment with different intervals (octave, twelfth, double octave, fifth) and with stopping points to determine which subdivisions tremble. Compare responses between gut-strings and metal-strings and between bowed/plucked and wind instruments to assess differences in sympathetic excitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopy sampling and quantification method (Leewenhoek)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate numbers of microscopic organisms by relating small sample volumes to common measures ('I suppose that a drop of water equals a pea... a little quantity... as large as a millet-grain... reckon the -gV part of a pea'), dividing samples, and scaling counts arithmetically/geometrically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect very small quantities (e.g., millet-grain-sized), place into a slender glass-pipe, divide that little water into ~25–30 parts, and observe one part after another; count organisms in a part and scale up by the known volume ratios (use cubing of diameters for 3D scaling). Present conservative estimates and consider alternative comparisons (grain of sand) to bound counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple microscopes and selective disclosure of instrument details
rubrics_metrics.description: Use different microscopes to detect forms of differing sizes and withhold description of superior instrument designs when necessary ('I still reserve to myself alone').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report which observations were possible only with higher-magnification instruments and note when certain instruments remain undescribed. Use comparative statements to justify claims about smaller organisms being visible only under stronger magnification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls in microscopy (distilled/boiled/thaw tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test distilled and boiled waters and observe effects of cold/thaw on microscopic life: 'examining also distilled and boiled waters... when the severe cold had killed the little creatures... the water thawed... after 24 hours... some living animals appeared again.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include control treatments (distillation, boiling, freezing) and report temporal reappearance or revival of organisms after thawing or warming; document timing (hours/days) to support claims about life, dormancy, or revival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting new-star ephemerides and magnitude changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a table/ephemeris exhibiting appearances and returns, 'its beginning and ending, how it has increased and decreased, when it disappeared, and when it shone out again.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record precise dated entries of observations, compare the new star's magnitude to nearby known stars (stating equalities or orders of magnitude), note phases/changes year-to-year, and document diligent searching during clear nights to confirm disappearances or reappearances. Use sustained watchful observation over many years to characterise variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting unusual meteors/comets
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting an unusual meteor: state the date/time, approximate duration, geographic distribution of observers, the appearance (brightness, shape, 'long appearance as of fire' with a 'great knob at the end'), and immediate behaviour (breaking into sparks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather corroborating reports from multiple counties/locations to assess whether the phenomenon was low or high and whether it moved swiftly; describe apparent luminosity relative to daylight/night ('equal to that of noon-day'), note short duration (less than half a minute), and cautiously propose conjectures about nature (comet passing near earth) while acknowledging the limits of rapid, surprised observation.
